title: Vali's death and Tara's lament
hook: an arrow from cover, and a question the tradition still discusses

segments.voice: Yesterday: the pact with Sugriva, tested: one arrow, seven sala trees. Did you ask an honest question instead of doubting quietly? Day five hundred eighty-six.

Two brothers fight at a city gate. A third man, hidden behind trees with a bow, shoots one of them. And the dying brother asks a question that tellers, poets and commentators have answered in different ways. The Ramayana doesn't make this scene easy. So today the job is simply to hear it as Valmiki tells it: who does what, who says what, and in what order. Where you land afterward is up to you; the tradition has room for more than one view.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS AT THE GATE.` → `AN ARROW FROM COVER.` → `THE DYING BROTHER'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sugriva goes to Kishkindha's gate and roars a challenge. Vali comes out, and the brothers fight. Rama, watching from cover with his bow drawn, doesn't shoot. The brothers look so alike that he can't tell them apart. Sugriva is beaten and flees: why didn't you shoot? Rama explains, and Lakshmana hangs a flowering creeper around Sugriva's neck, so Rama will know him. Second challenge. This time Vali's wife Tara stops him at the door. She's wise, and she's worried. Sugriva lost to you only today and he's back roaring, she says. He must have a powerful ally. I've heard it's Rama. Don't go. Vali goes anyway. Rama is righteous, he tells her; he won't do anything wrong. The fight begins, Vali starts to win, and Rama shoots. The arrow strikes Vali in the chest and he falls. Dying, Vali speaks to Rama, and it's an accusation. I wasn't fighting you. You struck from hiding while I fought someone else. What wrong had I done you? Rama answers him at length. This land is under the rule of Bharata's line, and I act for that rule. You took your brother's wife while he lived, a grave wrong. And kings hunt animals from cover. In the text, Vali accepts the answer and asks Rama's forgiveness. Some readers find Rama's answer sufficient. Others, including some commentators and poets, find the scene troubling, and some later tellings change it. Valmiki lets both the question and the answer stand. Tomorrow, Tara.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS TOO ALIKE TO TELL.` · `TARA'S WARNING.` · `THE ARROW FROM COVER.` · `VALI'S QUESTION, RAMA'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Sit with a question that doesn't resolve easily. Maybe one from today's story, maybe one from your own life. Breathe in, and let it be there. Breathe out, and don't answer it. Just notice what it feels like to hold a hard question without forcing it shut. Come back to the breath each time you start arguing with yourself. The bell holds the time.
Vali. King of Kishkindha, Sugriva's elder brother, shot by Rama's arrow today, who asks why and hears Rama's answer.
Your line: I wasn't fighting you. Today, when you disagree with someone, state the other side's best argument first. Day five hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Vali's death is discussed at length in Ramayana commentary; traditional commentators defend Rama's action in several ways, while some later tellings and modern readers question it.
